name: Buksa
world_status: a description exists but is not accessible
sweep_summary: Buksa (buks1238) is not in the catalog and the three works with stress in the title are pure noise: Glottolog has mis-assigned English-language clinical studies of prosody in autism/Williams syndrome (Shriberg et al. 2001; Plesa-Skwerer et al. 2007; Edelson et al. 2007) to this language; none concerns Buksa and none was downloaded. Glottolog's real descriptive record for Buksa (from its languoid JSON) is five items: Pant 2015 'Buksa/Buksari' (PLSI vol. 30(2), Orient Blackswan, 25 pp, the only phonology-level description - print only, high priority to acquire), its Hindi twin Pant 2014, Ghatak 2003 (ethnographic), Upreti 1900 and Nesfield 1885. I downloaded the two open ones from archive.org: Upreti 1900 (Hill dialects of the Kumaun division) gives a Bogsa (Tarai) folk-tale specimen and speaks only of dialects differing in 'accentuation' with no placement rule; Nesfield 1885 (Calcutta Review 80) is ethnographic with no stress statement. On-disk Schiering & van der Hulst 2010 lists Buksa genealogically only; Regmi 2014 mentions it only for lexical similarity with Tharu. Crossref title searches for Buksa/Bhoksa return only ethnographic, medical and agricultural papers. No first-hand word-stress statement for Buksa was read; no new stress statement was found.

earlier_scan.source_named: Glottolog buks1238 lists only Crooke 1896 (ethnographic subclassification note); no grammar, sketch, or phonology of Buksa located.

sources.citation: Language Division, Office of the Registrar General, India. Linguistic Survey of India: Uttar Pradesh (Census LSI series; PARI upload 2023).
sources.note: Buksa appears only in a Scheduled-Tribe mother-tongue table (Buksa: 4,710 persons, 4,664 returning Hindi); the volume's language sketches do not include Buksa.

sources.citation: Upreti, Gangadatta (1900). Hill dialects of the Kumaun division. Almora: Munshi Sadanand Sanwal. 135 pp.
sources.quote: These differences in the speech of the people may be referred, both to locality and to race. They consist very largely of varieties in accentuation, and etymology [...] The Bogsas, who claim to be Pawar Rajputs, and to have come from Banbasa (Oudh), and settled in the Tarai district [...] speak a strange dialect which is but an admixture of the plains and hill dialects.
sources.locator: Preface pp. (I)-(III) (the scanned text); Bogsa specimen the scanned text
sources.note: Gives a folk-tale specimen in the 'Bogsa (Tarai) dialect' in Devanagari and transliteration (pp. 93-97 of the book) but no stress rule; the preface only says the dialects differ 'very largely of varieties in accentuation, and etymology' and that the Bogsas 'speak a strange dialect which is but an admixture of the plains and hill dialects'. Silent on word-stress placement.

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.3, languoid buks1238 'Buksa' and reference search (sources.bib of Glottolog 5.1 CLDF held by the project).
sources.note: Bibliographic only. The six 'descriptive' refs listed in other than Pant 2014/2015 (Dyer et al. 2003, Nippold et al. 2005, Martin-Beltran et al. 2016, Chanseawrassamee & Shin 2009) are computerized mis-assignments from the word 'adolescents' and are not about Buksa. Genuine tkb-coded refs are all ethnographic/overview except Pant 2014, Pant 2015 and Hugoniot 2018.

sources.note: Nothing. Two paragraphs classing Bhuksa as a 'mongrel mixed dialect, made up of Hindostani, Braj Bhakha, and Kanauji, with an infusion of the Kumauni of the hills' (199,521 speakers), followed by a Prodigal Son specimen with remarks on case markers only; no accent or stress statement anywhere in the Bhuksa section.
